title: Captioned Phones for Hearing Loss: CapTel 840i, 880i and 2400i Compared
subtitle: How phones that show the other person's words on a screen work, who may qualify for free captioning, and what three CapTel models cost to buy.
excerpt: A captioned phone puts the caller's words on a screen so you can read along as you listen. Here is how the captioning service works, who may qualify, and how three CapTel phones compare.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Phone calls can be one of the first things to get hard when hearing starts to slip. In person, you can watch someone's face and lips. On the phone, all you have is a voice, and if it is soft, fast or muffled, you end up guessing or asking people to repeat themselves.
A captioned phone helps by showing the other person's words as text on a screen while you talk. You still hear the call, but you can read along to catch anything you missed.

A captioned phone looks much like a regular desk phone, with one big addition: a display that shows captions of what the caller says. In many modern models, the voices travel over the regular phone line, while the captions arrive over your home internet, according to HearingTracker.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has a consumer guide on this kind of service. It is an older, undated page, so treat it as general background. It says the service is for people with some hearing left:
"Captioned Telephone Service is used by persons with a hearing disability but some residual hearing." — FCC Consumer Guide: Telecommunications Relay Service

According to HearingTracker, the captioning service is funded by the federal Telecommunications Relay Service (TRS) Fund, and the phone and service are free to registered users who meet eligibility rules. The main rule is that you need hearing loss that makes captions necessary. Simply owning hearing aids does not qualify you on its own.

Registering may require a hearing-loss certification or a self-certification. A doctor or audiologist can help you work out whether you qualify. Only the registered person should turn captions on. Others in the household can use the phone with captions off. Confirm the exact rules with your captioning provider. HearingTracker also says the FCC generally limits each user to one active captioning provider.
Buying a CapTel phone outright does not get you around the eligibility rules. You still need to register to use captions.

items: Internet at home: captions need high-speed internet through Wi-Fi or a cable (called Ethernet). The 840i and 880i also need regular telephone service. If the internet goes down, the captions stop.
Screen size: larger screens and bigger caption text are easier on tired or low-vision eyes. Look at the screen size and how many font sizes you can choose.
Buttons versus touch screen: traditional phones with large physical buttons suit people who like the feel of a classic phone. A touch screen offers features like dialing by tapping a picture.
Volume boost: all three models here amplify sound by up to 40 dB, a measure of loudness.
Answering machine: a built-in machine that captions voicemail lets you read messages instead of replaying them.
Language: some models offer Spanish-to-Spanish captioning. The 2400i shows captions only on calls within the United States.
Warranty and returns: check what the seller offers. The 840i and 880i pages list a five-year manufacturer warranty and a 90-day money-back guarantee. The 2400i page does not state a warranty.
Setup help: ask whether installation help is included, especially if you are shopping for a parent who lives alone.
Price: other retailers may list different prices than the ones below, so check the current price before you buy.

sections.content: Setting It Up and Using It Well

Before the phone arrives, make sure the home Wi-Fi works reliably in the room where it will sit, and have the network name and password written down. Try to place the phone where light does not glare off the screen.

Once it is connected, adjust the caption size and colors until reading is comfortable. Then make a few practice calls with a family member so the new user can get comfortable listening and reading at the same time.

Keep in mind what captions cannot do. They help on the phone, not in face-to-face conversation, and they do not replace hearing aids. If you are unsure what kind of help suits your hearing, an audiologist or your doctor is a good place to start.

Captions depend on your internet connection, so plan for outages. We have not confirmed how captioned calls to 911 work, so ask your captioning provider before relying on captions for emergency calls. In any emergency, call 911.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A captioned phone will not fix every hearing challenge, but it can make phone calls easier to follow. Check eligibility first, confirm the internet is ready, and pick the screen that feels most comfortable.

products.name: CapTel 840i Captioned Phone
products.blurb: For anyone who wants a classic phone with large buttons and a 7-inch caption screen. It includes an answering machine, a five-year manufacturer warranty, a 90-day money-back guarantee and free installation help offered after order.

products.name: CapTel 880i Captioned Phone
products.blurb: Marketed for people with low vision as well as hearing loss, with a larger 10-inch caption screen. Captions can be switched on or off during a call, and it has a five-year manufacturer warranty and a 90-day money-back guarantee.

products.name: CapTel 2400i Touchscreen Captioned Phone
products.price: $99.95, marked down from $119.95 (HearWorld USA, November 2026); check current price
products.blurb: For those comfortable with a touch screen who would like to dial by picture. The page says captions appear automatically on incoming and outgoing calls and it captions voice messages, on US calls only.
